why_how.text: Drivers must watch carefully for pedestrians and be especially alert for young, elderly, disabled or intoxicated pedestrians, who are the most frequent victims of vehicle and pedestrian collisions.

Many pedestrian crashes come from pedestrians entering traffic carelessly, while others come from drivers failing to yield or failing to use caution, so drive slowly and stay alert wherever pedestrians are present.
When the vehicle ahead stops for a pedestrian, do not pass it even where two lanes are provided, because passing a stopped vehicle is a frequent cause of pedestrian deaths.
Watch for pedestrians walking against a red light, stepping out from between parked vehicles or crossing where there is no marked crosswalk, and yield to them even when they cross carelessly.
Never block a crosswalk with any part of the vehicle while stopped or waiting to turn, because that forces pedestrians to walk around you into danger.

Look for pedestrians every time your vehicle crosses a sidewalk or shoulder, for instance when pulling into or out of an alley, a driveway or a private road, and take extra care around playing children, who dart without checking traffic, and around elderly walkers, who may not sense the danger.
Do not stop to pick up hitchhikers on the interstate or its ramps.
A pedestrian who carries a white cane or walks with a guide dog and is crossing, or waiting to cross, the street in front of you requires you to come to a stop and give up the right-of-way.
A pedestrian with a white cane or a guide dog requires a full stop and yield, whereas other pedestrians require yielding without necessarily a stop.

When turning, look for and yield to pedestrians crossing side streets, many signalized intersections light up no turn on red signs during pedestrian crossing times, and you must never turn right on a red arrow.
At marked crosswalks a pedestrian sign may be placed in the road to remind drivers that they must yield to pedestrians within the crosswalk.

why_how.text: Bicyclists have the legal right to ride on all roads except where specially prohibited, such as limited access highways like the interstate, and the same traffic rules that apply to vehicle drivers apply to them.

Because bicycles are quieter and less visible, especially at night, a motorist should drive defensively around them, slow down when approaching, give plenty of room when passing, be ready to stop suddenly and not honk without good cause since the noise can startle the rider.

Bicyclists are allowed to ride as far to the left as needed for safety and may take the lane by riding toward its center because of hazards motorists cannot see or to position for the proper travel lane.

When passing a bicyclist keep a gap of at least four feet between the cyclist and your vehicle's right side, and on a road too narrow for the two of you side by side, hold back until you can pass without pushing the rider off the road.
A driver must leave at least four feet when passing a bicyclist, which is a clearance rule, distinct from the bicyclist's own right to use the whole lane when the road is too narrow to share.
Two bicyclists riding side by side are within the law, so reduce speed, let them adjust their position if they choose, and overtake only once it is safe to do so.
An oncoming bicyclist gets the same yield from a left turning driver that an oncoming motorist gets, and riders often travel faster than they seem, so leave them room.

Four common driver errors strike bicyclists: turning left without yielding to an oncoming cyclist, turning right without checking for a cyclist on the right going straight or leaving a sidewalk, entering or crossing a street without checking for a cyclist, and opening a door into a cyclist's path.
